Testimony in OPPOSITION to LD 436, An Act to Prohibit State Agencies from Promoting the COVID-19 Vaccination to Children
Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services March 31, 2025
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and esteemed members of the Committee on Health and Human Services,
I am Caroline Zimmerman, Chair of the Maine Immunization Coalition (MIC). The MIC is a network of associations, health care systems, and providers working to protect Maine people across their lifespan against vaccine-preventable diseases, by increasing immunization rates through information sharing and collaboration. Our coalition includes: Maine Chapter, American Academy of Pediatrics, MaineHealth, Maine Primary Care Association, Maine Public Health Association, Northern Light Health, Maine Families for Vaccines, Maine Community Action Partnership, Maine Medical Association, and Maine Osteopathic Association.
The MIC stands in strong opposition to LD 436, which seeks to prohibit any state departments and agencies from "promoting" the COVID-19 vaccine to anyone under the age of 18, through any means, including publicly accessible websites and educational materials. We are concerned this bill would unnecessarily restrict access to evidence-based information about the COVID-19 vaccine, promote antivaccine rhetoric, and aid in the spread of vaccine falsehoods.
Categorically and legislatively directing what our governing agencies can promote at any given point in time is a short-sighted response to a current social issue of distrust of science. Being able to have an evidence-informed discussion of prevention and treatment options, their risks and benefits, and how these options align with the patient's stated goals is foundational to providing health care to a population with diverse needs, beliefs, values, and medical conditions. This bill directly counters the ability of health care providers to share information that empowers their patients to make informed decisions that are best for them.
Information about the COVID-19 vaccine is publicly available online and through educational materials that are created and distributed by DHHS and Maine CDC. While these resources are not directly promoted to minors, they are publicly accessible, and therefore minors are able to access them like other members of the public. This bill could potentially limit public access to these digital and physical resources by attempting to prevent access to minors.

Commented [GU1]: strong opposition
Commented [GU2]: "short-sighted response that has the potential to exacerbate the current challenges with mistrust of science."
Commented [GU3]: The counter argument is that if they are publiccally available then no need to promote them.

State educational resources provide accurate, science-based information and recommendations on the COVID-19 vaccine that may be helpful to individuals deciding whether to get vaccinated. Any restriction to these resources threatens to create information voids, and if these voids are unaddressed, they allow misinformation about the COVID-19 vaccine to take root. Patients have important and valid information needs, and we must be able to answer their questions with evidence-based resources. Not doing so breeds further mistrust, confusion, and frustration with a health care system that is not responsive to their needs.
In conclusion, if passed, LD 436 would impede public access to information about the COVID-19 vaccine. We urge the committee to vote `Ought Not to Pass' on LD 436.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Caroline Zimmerman Chair, Maine Immunization Coalition

Testimony of the Maine Center for Disease Control
Maine Department of Health and Human Services
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
In opposition to LD 436, An Act to Prohibit State Agencies from Promoting the COVID-19
Vaccination to Children
Sponsor: Representative Eder
Hearing Date: March 31, 2025
Senator lngwersen, Representative Meyer, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Health and Human Services, my name is Jessica Shiminski, and I serve as the Program Director
of the Maine Immunization Program (MIP) within the Maine Center for Disease Control (Maine
CDC) in the Maine Department of Health and Human Services. I am here today to testify in
opposition to LD 436, An Act to Prohibit State Agencies fiom Promoting the COVID-I9
Vaccination to Children.
LD 436 seeks to prohibit state agencies from promoting the COVID-19 vaccination to children.
While the intent of this bill may be to limit government involvement in health decisions, the implications will be far reaching. This bill will create confusion and distrust among parents and
guardians, hindering efforts to increase vaccination rates among children. The Maine CDC will
need to focus further efforts and resources on combatting vaccine misinformation and managing
potential outbreaks. By limiting the availability of information about a healthcare choice that is proven to reduce COVID infection rates, Maine will likely see an increase in preventable
COVID-related illnesses and, consequently, the increased need for healthcareservices, including MaineCare-funded services.
The Maine CDC strongly opposes LD 436. Vaccine education and promotion are core functions
of the Maine Immunization Program (MIP). Reliable, science-based information for vaccines
(i.e. RSV, influenza, COVID, Tdap) is disseminated through trusted channels like provider
offices, Maine CDC and MaineCare websites, agency media campaigns, and professional
networking groups. While children under age 18 require parental consent to receive vaccinations,
trusted messaging from MIP and healthcare providers is essential in equipping parents and
guardians with accurate information to make informed decisions about their children's health.
Without this, misinformation will spread, and vaccination rates will decline, reversing the efforts that the Department has worked diligently to maintain.
This bill does not address a legitimate concern. Instead, it increases vaccine hesitancy and misinformation, posing a significant threat to public health. The State's efforts to increase vaccination rates are crucial in protecting the health of children in Maine and this bill
undermines those efforts. LD 436 explicitly prevents MaineCare from promoting the COVID-l9

vaccine to children, putting our most vulnerable populations, including MaineCare enrolled children and families, at greater risk of illness. Prohibiting education appears contrary to the fact
that MaineCare covers COVID vaccines for eligible children. This move will undoubtedly result
in an increase in healthcare costs for families and for the State.
In conclusion, Maine CDC, in partnership with the Department of Health and Human Services Office of MaineCare Services, strongly opposes LD 436, as it would interfere with the State's
ability to protect children from preventable diseases, limits families' access to credible information important to healthcare decision-making, and for the anticipated unintended consequences to public health, if enacted. Withholding this information, that would only serve to protect children, is denying people access to critical safety regulations that prevent harm. It
undermines the public's ability to make informed decisions, fails to prioritize patient safety, and compromises the Department's responsibility to protect the wellbeing of its youngest and most
vulnerable residents. We urge the committee to reject this bill to ensure Maine families continue
to have access to trusted, science-based information.
Thank you for your time and attention. I would be happy to answer any questions you may have and to make myself available for questions at the work session.

Testimony In Support of
LD 436 An Act to Prohibit State Agencies from Promoting the COVID-19 Vaccination to
Children
Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer and fellow members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Health and Human Services, my name is John Eder and I represent HD 136, the
town of Alfred and part of the towns of Lyman and Waterboro.

I am here to present LD 436 An Act to Prohibit State Agencies from Promoting the
COVID-19 Vaccination to Children. As we consider whether our beleaguered health agencies should continue recommending the COVID-19 vaccine for children, it's crucial that we
dispassionately appraise the evolving nature of the virus and the most recent evidence regarding vaccine safety in the interest of restoring public confidence in our health authorities.
The pandemic was declared over in 2023, and COVID-19 has attenuated to the point where
recent variants typically cause only mild cold or flu type symptoms. The CDC's February Data Tracker reported COVID-related emergency room visits in Maine were just 0.4% of total
visits["1].
The risk of severe illness in children was always extremely low, with a death rate of statistical
zero (<0.2%) during the pandemics peak['\2]. In fact, COVID-19 has always posed less danger
to children compared to all other respiratory illnesses,["3].
You'll recall that the rationale for mass vaccination of children was to prevent transmission to
older relatives. However, it is now well-established that COVID-19 vaccines never did prevent transmission["4]. By this fact alone, continuing to recommend this vaccine for children as

young as six months--who have never faced serious illness-~--lacks any discernible ethical or
scientific foundation at this point.
The accelerated development of COVID-l9 vaccines under Operation Warp Speed marked a
stark departure from traditional vaccine development timelines, which typically span 10 to l5
years["5]. The mRNA vaccines, never before tested on humans, were authorized in months. As
a result, we resorted post-marketing surveillance systems like VAERS and V--safe to identify long-term risks, despite the CDC acknowledging that only a small percentage of vaccine-related
injuries are reported to VAERS["6].
Analyses of the VAERS database revealed troubling data regarding severe adverse events
among children, including death, anaphylaxis, and myocarditis or pericarditis, particularly
among adolescent males['\7]. These risks, collected in VAERS are now acknowledged in the product information of Pfizer's COVID vaccine["8]. Given the data, the risk-to-benefit analysis
for children, especially babies as young as six months, seems upside down.
Yet on the Maine CDC's website, parents still encounter those erroneous claims, along with phrases like "protect your family" and "slow the spread," which continue to imply that the
vaccine stops transmission thought it does not [A9]. By highlighting outdated information and
not acknowledging the risks, our health authorities are failing to provide parents with the fully informed consent further destroying public trust.
Many parents do not realize that they cannot sue vaccine manufacturers for injury, as they are protected under the PREP Act["l0]. The Countermeasures Injury Compensation Program
(CICP) has been criticized for its low payouts and stringent criteria["1 1]. A recent court case in
Maine highlighted this issue. The PREP Act has been extended until 2029 [A12]. The childhood
vaccines remain under emergency use authorization, absent any emergency, implying that manufacturers seek to shield themselves from risk.
Unfortunately, deceptive marketing has been a hallmark of the pharmaceutical industry. The
ongoing opioid crisis in our state, which devastated communities and for which we received a
meager payout last year, was precipitated by Pharma knowingly pushing the overprescription of highly addictive OxyContin["13]. Lawmakers back then share responsibility; as agency
watchdogs, we must not repeat their mistake. Six states have presently joined a lawsuit against
Pfizer for claiming the vaccine stopped transmission and withholding crucial safety data about
pregnant women who suffered miscarriages after the shot['\l4].
VAERS reports hundreds of thousands of injuries and thousands of deaths attributed to the
vaccine["l 5]. A recent study from Yale highlighted immune system differences and the
continued presence of increasing spike protein two years after vaccination in those experiencing
what they've termed post-vaccination syndrome (PVS)["l 6]. We don't know what this
continued spike protein will do to children.

By the aforementioned metrics the vaccine is neither safe or effective--especially for children. Not surprisingly, only 21% of the whole population has received the 2024---25 COVID-l9
vaccine['\l 7]. People cited the well-known risks and the lack of need due to the attenuated virus. Ultimately, the truth can't be censored. American adults are abstaining, but children,
babies as young as six months old, rely on informed decisions made by their parents based on
infonnation they get from us.
Despite this Maine CDC is contracted to promote confidence and market the vaccine to parents
until 2027["18]. That contract in itself is not an ethically sound reason to continue promoting this vaccine for kids against the glaring evidence. Vaccine hesitancy overall is increasing post-
COVID [A19]. No amount of gaslighting or claims of misinformation are moving the needle in
the right direction of restoring trust. We need a different approach.
The absence of any emergency, the attenuated virus, the lack of transparency, the acknowledged risks, or the fact that it doesn't prevent transmission, undermine the basis for continued recommendations that children be vaccinated for COVID-19.
For many parents like myself, it is foreboding to see the vaccine recommended atop the
childhood vaccine schedule. Its presence there continues to erode the public's battered trust in
our public health authorities and sows distrust between parents and providers at a time when our
state is fast becoming a healthcare desert. My sincere hope is to foster an informed conversation
about our strategy and recalibrate our policies given all the current data.
Your ought-to-pass vote today will protect children and help restore trust.
Sincerely,
%/Mk.
John Eder
State Representative

Testimony in OPPOSITION to LD 436, An Act to Prohibit State Agencies from Promoting the COVID-19 Vaccination to Children
Joint Standing Committee on Health and Human Services
March 31, 2025
Senator lngwersen, Representative Meyer, and esteemed members of the Committee on Health and Human Services,
My name is Northe Saunders, and l serve as the Director of |\/laine Families for Vaccines and
the Executive Director of SAFE Communities Coalition. We work to promote vaccine
confidence and protect families from vaccine-preventable disease through strong, evidence-based public health policy.
I am here today to respectfully urge you to vote "Ought Not to Pass" on LD 436.
Anti-vaccine legislation like this should not advance in the legislature and has no place in
Maine.
This bill would prohibit state agencies from promoting the COVID-19 vaccine to anyone under 18---inc|uding through public websites or educational materials. In effect, it would censor accurate, science-based information and make it harder for Maine families to find trustworthy answers to their questions about COVID-19 vaccination.
As the father of three young children, I want accurate, trustworthy information when it
comes to my family's health. Like many parents, I'm not looking for pressure--l'm looking
for clarity. I want to understand the benefits, the risks, and the facts so I can make the best decision for my kids. That's especially true for something as often politicized as CO\/lD-19.
Empowering families like ours to make informed decisions about their health requires access to information we can use. If we don't respond to people's questions with good, accessible information, we create voids that get filled with confusion, speculation, or

outright misinformation. Public agencies have a responsibility to provide the public with
reliable, relevant resources--not to stay silent when people are looking for guidance.
Right now, Maine's state agency maintains publicly accessible, evidence-based information about COVID-19 vaccination--not targeted campaigns, but simple, factual resources that
parents, educators, providers, and even teens can use to make informed choices.
This bill doesn't solve a problem--it creates one. It adds confusion. It interferes with good public health communication. And it moves us further away from a culture where people feel empowered to take charge of their health.

urge you to reject LD 436.

10040985:
March 30, 2025

Re: LD 436, An Act to Prohibit State Agencies from Promoting the COVID-19 Vaccination to Children

To: Senator Ingwersen, Representative Meyer, and the members of the Health and Human Services Committee

The Maine Chapter of the Freedom From Religion Foundation (MC-FFRF) is writing AGAINST LD 436, An Act to Prohibit State Agencies from Promoting the COVID-19 Vaccination to Children.

I should be shocked and disappointed that such testimony is necessary, but it is a sign of the times that I am not. One of the most effective tools we have to combat COVID-19 is vaccination. The approval and widespread distribution of COVID-19 vaccines has reduced the severity of illness, prevented hospitalizations, and saved lives. LD 436 is not only harmful but also shortsighted, as it disregards public health, undermines efforts to control the spread of the virus, and puts our children at unnecessary risk.

Children are less likely to experience severe illness compared to adults, but COVID-19 can still lead to serious complications including hospitalization, long-term health issues, and even death. By prohibiting the promotion of COVID-19 vaccines for children, we are denying them a safe and effective preventive measure. Protecting children from the worst outcomes of COVID-19 should be a top priority. Restricting vaccine promotion limits this protection.

One of the most important reasons to vaccinate children is to reduce the overall spread of the virus. Children can be asymptomatic carriers. This is especially concerning when children interact with vulnerable populations who may be more at risk of severe illness. Vaccinating children reduces the number of potential carriers and limits the ability of the virus to spread. Prohibiting the promotion of COVID-19 vaccines for children undermines efforts to achieve widespread immunity, which is essential to controlling the pandemic. Without widespread vaccination of children, the goal of controlling COVID-19 will be out of reach.

The vaccines authorized for use in children have undergone rigorous clinical trials. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) continue to monitor the safety of COVID-19 vaccines through ongoing surveillance and studies. The benefits of vaccination far outweigh the risks, which are rare and typically mild, such as temporary soreness at the injection site or mild fever.

Maine Chapter, Freedom From Religion Foundation PO Box 161 Vassalboro, ME 04989-0161

President.RV@ffrfmaine.org phone: 207-370-8813 www.ffrfmaine.org

Prohibiting the promotion of these vaccines ignores the scientific consensus and evidence that supports their use. Public health guidance should be based on the best available science, which overwhelmingly supports the vaccination of children as an important measure to protect public health. We cannot let political or ideological motivations override the science that has been instrumental in reducing the harm caused by COVID-19.
Vaccinating children against COVID-19 is a critical step in ensuring that schools can remain open and that children can have a more normal educational experience.
Prohibiting the promotion of COVID-19 vaccines for children could create a situation in which children who are not vaccinated may be more likely to contract and spread COVID-19, leading to more outbreaks in schools and further disruptions to education. Promoting vaccination among children is an essential part of ensuring that children are not deprived of the educational and social experiences they need to thrive.
One of the great challenges has been the spread of misinformation about COVID-19 vaccines. Many people are distrustful of vaccines due to misleading or false information. By prohibiting the promotion of COVID-19 vaccines for children, we undermine public health campaigns and allow misinformation to get traction. The promotion of COVID-19 vaccines for children is not just about providing accurate information; it's also about countering harmful myths and promoting trust in the healthcare system. Public health officials and medical professionals have a responsibility to provide children and their families with the ability to make informed decisions. Preventing the promotion of vaccines contradicts this goal.
The decision to vaccinate children is not just about individual health; it is a collective responsibility to protect the most vulnerable members of society.
Prohibiting the promotion of COVID-19 vaccines for children prioritizes a narrow view of individual freedom over the broader public health goal of minimizing harm to everyone. Vaccinating children is one of the most effective ways to reduce the spread of COVID-19 and ensure that we can protect those who are most at risk.
For these reasons, the MC-FFRF asks the committee to vote "OUGHT NOT TO PASS" to ensure that accurate, science-based information is available to everyone. Thank you for your time and consideration.
-Ray Vensel, President

Maine Chapter, Freedom From Religion Foundation PO Box 161 Vassalboro, ME 04989-0161

recommendations. While the vaccine does decrease a child's risk of hospitalization by
57% (Pediatrics (2023) 151 (4)): it offers little protection against the usual mild but annoying

against severe illness.
Another issue on some parents' (and physicians') minds is "long COVID" (PASC). This puzzling condition can occur after even mild cases of COVID and is currently
under intense study. It can occur in childhood, and again the vaccine cuts down the risk by half. Pediatrics (2024) 153 (4). Families who have experienced PASC more often
choose the shot.
